newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire politicians in deadlock on new government.
newsitem.headline: Zaire politicians in deadlock on new government.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko may appoint a prime minister if the political parties fail to meet his Monday deadline to form a crisis government to deal with the rebel war in the eastern region, senior aides said.
Mobutu's spokesman told Reuters on Sunday the president could invoke special emergency war-time powers to name a new prime minister if the extended deadline was not met.

"The president is open to all possiblities, but what he hoped for was unity to face the war in the east, because if political leaders remain divided it will only serve the rebels' cause," spokesman Kabuya Lumuna said.
"But now we have a war of posts in the government, instead of a united front against the war in the east," he said.

The political parties, grouped in two main alliances that represent parties in parliament, missed a Saturday deadline as they squabbled among themselves on picking someone to lead a government to handle the Rwandan-backed rebel war.

Three main candidates are vying to lead the government -- incumbent Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, and the head of a breakaway faction of his UDPS party, Frederic Kibassa Maliba.
Zaire's ruler of 31 years returned to the capital on Tuesday after almost four months of convalescence in Europe where he underwent surgery for cancer.

He immediately reshuffled the military high command, bringing in a popular general, Mahele Lieko Bokungo, with extra powers over the entire armed forces to try and retake territory from ethnic Tutsi rebels in eastern Zaire.
On Thursday he gave political leaders 48 hours to nominate a crisis government but later extended this.

In the working class Matonge neighbourhood of the capital where Tshisekedi commands huge support, UDPS militants threatened a catastrophe if their leader was not named prime minister, a post he held briefly a few years ago before Mobutu sacked him.

"If tomorrow Kengo maintains power we will march and march in the streets until he has to resign. There will be many deaths and President Mobutu himself will never return to Europe for treatment," said resident Frederic Simpa.

The militants, who gather daily in the district, expressed support for the message of Laurent Kabila, the Rwandan-backed rebel leader who says he is fighting to bring to an end decades of one-man rule by Mobutu.
But they said that if Tshisekedi was re-appointed the war in the east, which erupted in Mobutu's absence, would soon end.

"Tshisekedi is known for his respect of the laws, and for being the only consistent opponent of the regime. He represents the hope of the people, and if they allow him to work again, Kabila will stop what he is doing in the east immediately," said Faustin Kalala, a 36-year-old mechanic.
Further negotiations between political parties were due on Sunday afternoon and there were unconfirmed reports from the UDPS that Tshisekedi would be meeting the president.

Mobutu met at length on Saturday with Kengo, who enjoys the support of Western countries for his attempts over the past two years to reform Zaire's corrupt economy. Opposition members say France, which has backed Mobutu at difficult times, is exerting pressure on the president to keep Kengo.
